content.title: Let private Conversations at one Destination reach each other
content.intent: This PR adds a same-Destination access rule, so Junior threads in one private Slack channel, DM, or group DM can find, read, and message each other.

chapters.caption: One rule decides whether a Conversation may reach another
chapters.body: Before this PR, the access policy had three rows: same Conversation tree allows, public target allows, any other private target is denied [1]. The code keeps both allow branches: the same-tree check [2] and the public fallback [3].
asks: Does the person running the Turn affect the result?

chapters.caption: Threads in one private channel were walled off from each other
chapters.body: Top-level agent search returned only public roots [1]. A private sender could not message any other top-level agent [2]. So two Junior threads in the same private channel could not find or message each other, even though the same people see both.
asks: Could a private thread reach anything outside its own tree?

chapters.caption: Access rows carry the root's Destination, and a matching one allows
chapters.body: ConversationAccess gains an optional destinationId [1]. The shared reader selects it from the root's Destination [2] and sets it only when the stored tree is valid [3]. canAccessConversation adds a check after the same-tree one: equal Destination ids allow [4].

decisions.question: Does one Destination always mean one audience, also when private-channel membership changes or visibility is 'unknown'?

asks: What if either side has no Destination?
Does row 2 look at visibility at all?

chapters.caption: Top-level search also returns roots at the requester's Destination
chapters.body: The file doc now states the new scope [1]. The search adds an OR: public, or the same destinationId as the requester row [2]. Only roots can search top_level, so this matches the root Destination used by the access rule. The test adds a second thread in the private channel [3] and expects search to find it [4].
asks: Can a conversation_ids filter add a private target?

chapters.caption: messageAgent allows same-Destination private targets
chapters.body: The access check now goes through canAccessConversation first, and the private-to-public write block runs only when the receiver is public [1]. The test helper gains a thread timestamp to make a second thread in one channel [2][3]. The private neighbor gets the message, and a public sender still cannot reach it [4].

evidence.note: Write block only for public receivers

asks: Can a private thread still write into a public one?
Can a child agent use this?

chapters.caption: Tool descriptions tell the model about same-channel reach
chapters.body: The messageAgent description now allows two conversations in one private channel or DM [1]. The searchAgents relation, scope, and tool descriptions say the same [2][3][4]. These strings are what the model reads, so they decide whether it tries the new path.

chapters.caption: Web and local Conversations keep their own Destination
chapters.body: A web or local Conversation gets a local Destination keyed by its own id, so row 2 does not widen it [1]. This code is unchanged by the PR. But Continue in Slack can replace a web root's stored Destination [2], which then puts it under row 2.

evidence.note: Web gets its own local Destination

decisions.question: A private web root continued in a private Slack channel then shares that Destination. Is that the intended reach?

asks: Do web forks or Quick questions share their source's Destination?

chapters.caption: The policy doc adds row 2 and updates the write and surface rules
chapters.body: The intent now names Visibility and Destination as the boundaries [1]. The table adds row 2 and explains what one Destination means [2]. Writes from private Conversations now go only to the same Destination [3], and searchAgents top_level is listed as a surface [4].

chapters.caption: Event reads switch from their own root walk to the shared access reader
chapters.body: assertCanReadConversationEvents used to walk parents in the Conversation store to find each root [1]. Now it loads both Conversations through the shared SQL reader, so it gets the Destination and the same tree checks as other callers [2]. A requester that is not stored now reaches only public targets.

decisions.question: The shared reader denies a tree whose stored root_conversation_id is inconsistent. Could the old parent walk have allowed rows now denied?

asks: Is this one query or two?

chapters.caption: A same-DM neighbor reads events; other surfaces are still denied
chapters.body: The existing test still shows a private DM Conversation is denied to other surfaces [1]. A new case records a second Conversation in the same DM and reads the first one's events [2]. The unit test of the rule has one case per policy row, including the same and different Destination cases [3].
asks: Is a missing Conversation still indistinguishable from a private one?

splits.reason: Mixes the same-Destination access feature with a refactor of event-read access onto the shared SQL reader.
